meta.andy-electric.desc: Andy Electric case study: branding and website for an electrical services company in the USA.
andy-electric.t004: I worked as a Brand & UX Designer with an end-to-end approach, integrating AI tools (Claude Code, Figma) to speed up production and improve consistency between UX design and technical implementation.
andy-electric.t005: Analysis of the company's positioning and business needs.
andy-electric.t006: Definition of a new artistic and strategic direction.
andy-electric.t007: Design of the visual identity and its applications.
andy-electric.t012: The electrical services sector in the United States is worth several billion dollars and remains largely dominated by local players with low digital maturity.
andy-electric.t013: 80%+ of customers search for local services online before contacting a company.
andy-electric.t014: The first digital impression strongly influences trust and the decision to get in touch.
andy-electric.t015: An optimized web presence can significantly increase lead generation.
andy-electric.t016: In this context, the lack of a structured website and a strong brand identity meant a significant loss of business opportunities for Andy Electric.
andy-electric.t023: Share of the addressable market online.
andy-electric.t027: Of leads coming from word of mouth.
andy-electric.t029: Of customers with no digital access to the company.

andy-electric.t032: Analysis of context and business needs
andy-electric.t034: Definition of a brand and product strategy
andy-electric.t037: Goal: improve brand perception and generate commercial opportunities.
andy-electric.t038: Creating an acquisition and conversion channel
andy-electric.t039: The company had no structured website to present its services and convert visitors. I designed and built a website focused on clarity of the offer, building trust and user conversion.
andy-electric.t045: The website thus becomes a real entry point for potential customers.
andy-electric.t048: Consistent visual identity across all touchpoints (online & offline)
andy-electric.t050: Production time optimized thanks to the integration of AI tools

meta.bellpi.title: Bellpi, Case study · Alejandro Guevara
meta.bellpi.desc: Bellpi case study: e-commerce platform for used vehicles in Colombia.
bellpi.t004: Bellpi is an innovative e-commerce platform for buying and selling used vehicles in Colombia, aiming to turn a traditionally complex experience into a fully user-centered, 100% digital journey.
bellpi.t005: As a UX & Service Designer, I contributed to the launch of version 1 of the platform and to its successive iterations:
bellpi.t006: Designing and optimizing end-to-end user journeys for buyers and sellers.
bellpi.t007: Conducting user research and turning findings into actionable insights.
bellpi.t008: Collaborating with cross-functional teams to align design decisions with business goals.
bellpi.t009: Creating wireframes, prototypes and service blueprints to visualize and validate the proposed solutions.
bellpi.t011: I worked in a multidisciplinary team where, from the initial product launch, we set clear OKRs and KPIs to monitor performance and guide iterative development. This structured approach led to a second phase focused on user empathy, in which we evaluated the user journeys designed for sellers and buyers.
bellpi.t016: My role also involved adapting the platform to several formats, mobile totems, tablets, desktops and touchscreens, while keeping a consistent user experience.
bellpi.t018: UX research and analysis revealed key insights that guided the continuous improvement of the platform. I played a strategic role in turning these findings into actionable design solutions, aligning user needs with company goals.
bellpi.t019: Through close collaboration with developers and stakeholders, I ensured consistency across touchpoints while focusing on accessibility, information architecture and usability in an agile environment.
bellpi.t021: In parallel, I also contributed to evaluating and improving the physical experience. This involved running observation sessions, in-depth analysis and spatial modeling of the layout and flows within Bellpi's first physical location.
bellpi.t028: As part of the UX design process, I contributed to creating a responsive web experience optimized for touch interactions, specifically for use at events and trade shows. The goal was to ensure intuitive navigation, quick understanding and accessible interaction in public, high-traffic environments.
bellpi.t033: Bellpi, touchscreen kiosks and interactive experience
meta.bnf.title: Musée de la BnF, Case study · Alejandro Guevara
meta.bnf.desc: Musée de la BnF case study: digital twin web app for the architectural heritage and collections of the Richelieu site.
bnf.t004: A web application designed to create a digital twin showcasing the architectural heritage and collections of the Richelieu site of the Bibliothèque nationale de France. The project aims to offer an immersive cultural experience combining a 3D virtual tour, discovery of the collections and streaming of documentary content.
bnf.t005: Context analysis and on-site user research
bnf.t006: Definition of scenarios and user journeys
bnf.t007: Design of flows and information architecture
bnf.t010: An in-depth comparative analysis was carried out to identify best practices in digital cultural experiences. The references include 3D virtual tour apps, cultural streaming platforms and museums that have developed innovative digital experiences.
bnf.t012: Four user profiles were defined from field research and interviews with visitors to the Richelieu site. These personas guided every design decision throughout the project.
bnf.t014: Collection proposal, Explore the museum's current, past and upcoming exhibitions. Access the collections room by room and discover the artworks on display.
bnf.t015: Collections room tour, Explore the museum's evolution over time through the interactive map. A virtual tour allows a detailed discovery of each room.
bnf.t019: Allow users to enjoy the content created by the museum through cultural streaming and share it remotely with others. A built-in chat and audio system encourages real-time interaction between participants.
bnf.t021: A complete proposal bringing together streaming of heritage documentaries, navigation of the interactive 3D map and exploration of the collections, all combined in one coherent digital experience.
bnf.t023: Benchmark, comparative analysis of digital references
bnf.t025: Exhibitions and collections of the BnF museum
bnf.t026: 3D tour of the museum and its collections
bnf.t027: User journey, buying tickets, physical visit

meta.jumbomana.title: JumboMana, Case study · Alejandro Guevara
meta.jumbomana.desc: JumboMana case study: AI assistant guiding travelers at Lyon-Saint-Exupéry International Airport.
jumbomana.t004: The challenge was to design a clear, engaging experience able to capture attention in such a busy environment without being mistaken for advertising. The interface had to enable a quick understanding of its features, ensure smooth use and effectively complement the airport's existing information systems.
jumbomana.t005: Offer an intuitive, accessible service able to serve millions of travelers with different needs and languages.
jumbomana.t006: Reduce user resistance through a friendly avatar and natural interaction (touch or voice).
jumbomana.t007: Improve wayfinding with interactive maps, QR codes and precise, contextual answers.
jumbomana.t009: How effectively would the system complement the airport's traditional information services, without causing confusion or resistance among users, while remaining recognizable, understandable and accessible?
jumbomana.t011: Visitors, travelers, companions, looking for information, directions or assistance.
jumbomana.t013: During a trip through the airport, when real-time directions or information are needed.
jumbomana.t015: Lyon-Saint-Exupéry Airport, transit areas, arrival and departure halls, services.
jumbomana.t017: Multi-format conversational AI assistant, touch kiosk and mobile app.
jumbomana.t019: We structured our design process with a collaborative tool to map user insights, prioritize key features and validate design hypotheses. This approach helped align the team and make informed decisions at every stage of the project.
jumbomana.t021: The project included two interface versions: one for mobile devices and another designed for large touchscreens. The storyboard helped us determine how users would navigate each version, focusing on key moments of interaction, accessibility and flow consistency.
jumbomana.t023: During testing, participants successfully interacted with the key features: muting the sound, changing the language, searching for a restaurant and finding the route to the selected restaurant.
jumbomana.t025: These results indicate that the interface was generally intuitive and helped users reach their goals with minimal friction.

meta.paramo.title: ParamoTotem, Case study · Alejandro Guevara
meta.paramo.desc: ParamoTotem case study: an immersive, interactive experience inspired by the natural ecosystems of the Colombian páramo.
paramo.t003: An experimental project designed to create an immersive, interactive experience inspired by the natural ecosystems of the Colombian páramo, through thematic stations dedicated to each emblematic species.
paramo.t010: The páramo is one of the most precious and most threatened ecosystems on the planet. ParamoTotem is an interactive installation that immerses visitors in this unique environment through stations dedicated to each emblematic species: the spectacled bear, the Andean condor, the frailejón and the orchid.
paramo.t011: Each station is designed as a self-contained sensory space, combining generative visuals, ambient sounds and physical interactions to create a strong emotional bond with the páramo's biodiversity.
paramo.t013: The four stations form a narrative and sensory journey. Each one explores a páramo species through specific interactions and its own visual identity, while keeping the experience coherent as a whole.
paramo.t019: Generative visuals are at the heart of the ParamoTotem experience. Lights, textures and animations respond to visitors' interactions, creating a living, evolving atmosphere that reflects the dynamics of natural ecosystems.

meta.ublo.title: Ublo, Case study · Alejandro Guevara
meta.ublo.desc: Ublo case study: property management platform in France.
ublo.t004: As a UX Designer on the Ublo team, a France-based property management platform with over 2,000 users and 20 clients across the country, my role was to continuously improve the interface and the overall user experience.
ublo.t005: I worked iteratively on more than 15 new features and 20 platform improvements, delivering continuous enhancements directly aligned with customer feedback and business requirements.
ublo.t007: I explored the use of artificial intelligence tools in the design and research phases, from AI-assisted analysis of user behavior to interaction prototyping and streamlined content generation.
ublo.t008: Throughout the process, I carried out:
ublo.t009: Technical research to understand the system's limits and opportunities.
ublo.t010: Comparative analysis to identify best practices and market standards.
ublo.t011: User journey mapping and user stories to structure logical, effective solutions.
ublo.t013: I carried out a full UX audit of the platform to identify the main friction points and align the user experience with business goals. The analysis relied on a heuristic evaluation (Nielsen, Bastien & Scapin), a study of key user journeys, information architecture, visual consistency and accessibility (WCAG), complemented by analytics data analysis.
ublo.t014: Key UX principles guided every proposal:
ublo.t016: Nature and priority of the information architecture
ublo.t017: Clear hierarchy of content and interface elements
ublo.t018: Identification of the user's key actions
ublo.t019: Optimized interaction patterns between the user and the interface

ublo.t029: I wrote clear UX copy and produced all the supporting documentation, providing complete design specifications and screens ready to hand over to the development team. To strengthen our decision-making, I introduced and tracked key UX KPIs:

qualnet.role: French quality software publisher · Imagine Human group
qualnet.p1: Qualnet is a French quality software publisher founded in 1997, which joined the Imagine Human group in 2026. Its no-code solutions help private and public organisations simplify, structure and manage their quality processes.
qualnet.p2: The suite covers quality document management (Qualnet DOC), process digitalisation (Qualnet DYNAMIC) and quality management: non-conformities, audits, action plans, supplier evaluation and KPIs. It is available as SaaS or on-premise and used in healthcare, food, pharma, banking and insurance, and industry.
qualnet.p3: I work there as Product Owner. I manage the backlog and run two-week sprints focused on continuous product improvement.

qualnet.chiff.meta: Qualnet DYNAMIC · Framing kicked off on 19/10/2026 (sprint 323) · 360° framing method
qualnet.chiff.p1: Some clients, bound by strict rules on attachments, must prevent any unauthorised person from accessing the files stored on their server. The goal: let a Qualnet DYNAMIC administrator turn on attachment encryption with a global Yes / No option, knowing what changes before and after turning it on, and being able to check that encryption is actually active.
qualnet.chiff.s1p: I framed the topic on a single page shared with the team: goals, why, for whom, KPIs, risks and dependencies.
qualnet.chiff.s1l1: For whom: DYNAMIC administrators (Qualnet support or client admins), with no change expected for end users.
qualnet.chiff.s1l2: KPIs: number of clients who turn the option on at 3 and 6 months, and zero "unreadable attachment" or "option has no effect" tickets.
qualnet.chiff.s1l3: Risks: lost or mishandled keys, documents already uploaded, processing time and switching back to "No".
qualnet.chiff.s2p: To decide which dialog to offer, I analysed how Nextcloud, Dropbox, Windows BitLocker, GitHub and Amazon S3 present a high-impact action: what we observe, what we like and what we like less.
qualnet.chiff.s2l1: Must have: state the scope (new documents only, or existing ones too) and the consequences before confirming.
qualnet.chiff.s2l2: Buttons that describe the action ("Turn on encryption") rather than Yes / No.
qualnet.chiff.s2l3: Chosen: Nextcloud's impact summary and BitLocker's scope choice.
qualnet.chiff.s3p: I mapped the administrator's journey in 8 steps, from opening the settings to checking encryption, then the full flow: screens, dialogs, actions and statuses. 10 friction points were spotted and prioritised before designing, to be validated with the development team.
qualnet.chiff.s4p: The mock-ups cover every state of the option: not encrypted, encryption in progress, encrypted, processing failure and verification. Each screen comes with notes for developers: impact dialogs, retry after a failure, status badge and progress tooltip.
qualnet.chiff.img.bench: Benchmark summary: which dialog to offer?
qualnet.chiff.img.storymap: Story map of the encryption journey
qualnet.chiff.img.maquettes: Mock-ups of the chosen solution with developer notes

spotify.title: Spotify
spotify.role: Rethinking three moments of the Spotify experience
spotify.ctx.lead: Redesigning Spotify because the experience is not just about listening to music.
spotify.ctx.body: UX/UI bootcamp project at Coderhouse: rethinking three moments of the Spotify app based on what its users really experience, from the survey to the final screens. The case starts with the result, the three features, then tells how I got there by designing and testing.
spotify.ctx.r1: Survey and analysis of the answers
spotify.ctx.r4: Task flows, user flows and wireflows
spotify.research.b: It all starts with a survey of 11 users aged 25 to 31. They like the app, but three gaps keep coming up.
spotify.research.l1: Sharing an opinion, most would like to rate and comment on what they just listened to.
spotify.research.l2: Finding help, many struggled to find technical information in the app.
spotify.research.l3: Keeping what you like, saving and sorting content takes too many steps.
spotify.research.l4: 100% use the paid version: every friction hits subscribers.
spotify.research.lead: The problem isn't the app, it's what's missing around listening.
spotify.persona.b1: To put a face on the survey answers, I created a persona: Daniela Salazar, 28, an environmental engineer and master's student. Her saved card has a problem, her monthly subscription is suspended, and she wants to reactivate it before boarding a plane so she can listen to her music during the flight.
spotify.persona.b2: Her user journey shows where the experience breaks: no help in the app, a web search, a device switch, a step-by-step tutorial, then a new login. Mood drops at every step.
spotify.persona.lead: Every time users leave the app, the experience gets worse.
spotify.alt.journey: Daniela's user journey: support, switching sites, step by step, payment method
spotify.tasks.b: The survey and the user journey produced three tasks to design, each tied to an identified gap:
spotify.tasks.l1: Change the payment method without leaving the app.
spotify.tasks.l2: Rate and comment on a podcast you have just listened to, and read what others think.
spotify.tasks.l3: Save a song to the playlist of her choice in a few taps.
spotify.ia.b: Before drawing anything, I reworked the information architecture. The profile now holds every setting, from payment method to technical support, and the library gathers playlists, podcasts, albums and downloaded content. The goal: every answer sits where users look for it.
spotify.flow.b: Each task followed the same path, from the most abstract to the most concrete:
spotify.flow.l1: Task flow, the ideal steps: the user finishes an episode, picks a rating and publishes an opinion.
spotify.flow.l2: User flow, the decisions and possible paths: add a comment or only send the rating.
spotify.flow.l3: Wireflow, the same decisions laid out on low fidelity screens.
spotify.flow.l4: Wireframes, the key screens of each task, such as the card form, before moving to the UI.
spotify.alt.flows: Task flow, user flow and wireflow: rating a podcast
spotify.alt.wire: Low fidelity wireframes for changing the payment method
spotify.tests.b: The prototype was tested with 5 participants aged 25 to 35, all working and comfortable with technology: an industrial designer, a filmmaker, a fitness coach, a chef and a graphic designer.
spotify.tests.l1: Validate, check whether our assumptions about user behaviour hold up against the prototype.
spotify.tests.l2: Analyse, understand how they interact with the product and spot what to improve.
spotify.tests.l3: Learn, get to know our users and how they use the redesigned product.
spotify.learn.l1: The journey also plays out off screen. The worst moments of the user journey came when users had to leave the app: the answer was to bring everything back inside.
spotify.learn.l2: Three needs, one thread. Payment, saving and reviews all start from the same finding: users should be able to act without leaving the app.
spotify.learn.l3: Next step: measure success rate and time per task in a new round of tests.
spotify.feat.b: Here is the result. Each feature answers a gap identified with users.
spotify.feat.1.b: A defined space where users can manage several account settings.
spotify.feat.1.b2: Payment method management to make changing or updating it easy, all from the same device.
spotify.feat.2.b: Make saving songs as easy as possible and let users choose where to put them.
spotify.feat.3.b: Read other users' opinions on the same content and interact with them.
spotify.board.song: Few steps to save things in an organized way
spotify.board.comm: Rate and share your opinion in a community
spotify.note.pay3: Support the user at every moment they need help.
spotify.note.song2: Efficiency for the user: in three actions, the song is saved.
spotify.note.comm1: Let users rate and comment on the content they just listened to.
spotify.det.b: Spotify is a music platform created in 2008, first as a streaming player for computers. It now has a 4.7 out of 5 rating and more than 2.9 million user comments.
spotify.det.m3l: countries where the iOS app is available.
spotify.det.v1: Trust: build trust between users and the app, conveying calm around how the subscription payment is handled.
spotify.det.v2: Ease: let users manage several features of their profile from the app, with personalization and several support channels available at any time.
spotify.det.v3: Community: create a community where the content is of the best quality, encouraging user opinions so that everyone contributes and feels included.
spotify.det.p1: Design for people: the visual look must convey clarity and accessibility, since the app is used by millions of people worldwide.
spotify.det.p2: Design to evolve: every element of the design system has a conceptual base and can evolve with the brand while staying consistent.
spotify.det.p3: Design to convey: what is needed, when it is needed. Content must be clear, simple and organized, and guide users at every moment.
spotify.det.p4: Design to make things easy: every piece is part of a complex, unified system, with no isolated components or features.
spotify.how.b: Everything above came out of a process: designing, testing and adjusting. Here is how, from the methodology to the product's voice.
spotify.alt.principes: Shared purposes and values (trust, ease, community) and four design principles
spotify.alt.palettes: Color palettes: white, cool gray, raspberry, orange, green, blue, coral and black, in five tones
spotify.alt.components: Components: tab bar, player elements, song and settings lists, bank card and podcast covers

spotify.alt.taskC: Task C: task flow, user flow and wireflow for updating the payment method
spotify.alt.voice: Voice matrix: quality, efficiency, closeness and clarity
spotify.alt.tone: Tone matrix: from the home screen to the save confirmation, between friendly and serious
spotify.alt.style: Style guide: date, success and error messages, content information, description and input fields
spotify.hyp.b1: I chose Spotify in its mobile version because its navigation, the information about content and the place users have in rating that content can be simplified. The hypothesis: users who easily find quality content and share their point of view help build communities around music and podcasts.
spotify.hyp.b2: To test it, the work follows the five planes of user experience:
spotify.hyp.b3: To understand the motivations, expectations and pain points of real users, I combined four tools: surveys, interviews, heuristic analysis and laws of UX.
spotify.mkt.b: Before talking to users, I placed the app in its market: a huge base, mostly free, with a well represented 25 to 34 age group.
spotify.mkt.m2l: active users on the free version.
spotify.mkt.m3l: active users on the paid version.
spotify.mkt.m5l: split in % between men and women in the user base.
spotify.mkt.b2: On top of that, 11 million artists and creators feed the catalogue.
spotify.research.b2: Two qualitative surveys of 11 people each and 5 interviews went further. Among the people reached, 11 are between 25 and 31 and 5 between 18 and 24.
spotify.research.m1l: of the people interviewed would like to leave a comment on the content they consume.
spotify.research.m3l: have struggled to find a saved song.
spotify.research.m4l: are satisfied with the app's features.
spotify.research.m5l: people mainly use Spotify while travelling.
spotify.research.m6l: of the people surveyed and interviewed have the paid version.
spotify.research.q1: “When I had a problem with my payment method, I had to go to a website that didn't inspire trust.”
spotify.research.q2: “I don't know where my things are saved.”
spotify.research.q3: “I never found a help section in the app, I had to watch a video on YouTube.”
spotify.research.q4: “I save songs and podcasts, but finding them afterwards is a problem.”
spotify.research.q5: “I can't see what people say about a new podcast.”
spotify.persona.pl1: Her goals: quickly find the songs and podcasts she wants, see what others think to decide, and solve a problem without looking for help elsewhere.
spotify.persona.pl2: What drives her: music goes with her through every moment, and she likes to learn and share her finds with friends, for whom she is the DJ.
spotify.persona.pl3: Her frustrations: not seeing what others think of a piece of content, not finding help when the app fails, no longer knowing where her songs are saved.
spotify.opp.l1: Looking for help: find answers and be guided inside the app, through a chatbot, a call or a written or video FAQ.
spotify.opp.l2: Switching site: avoid leaving the app and allow search by keywords, categories or topics tied to its features.
spotify.opp.l3: Following the steps: no device switch and no new login, since the user is already signed in.
spotify.opp.l4: Payment method: offer another way to load card data (by photo), ask where to receive the confirmation and notify from the app that the problem is solved.
spotify.lean.b: To frame the problem, look for solutions and prepare the experiments that test my assumptions, I filled in a Lean UX canvas.
spotify.lean.l1: Problem: changing the payment method means going to an external page, artists and podcasts can't be commented on, and saved songs are hard to locate.
spotify.lean.l2: User personas: listeners aged 18 to 35 on mobile, entrepreneurs who set the mood of their spaces with music, and people aged 40 to 60 who want to stay informed in a simple way.
spotify.lean.l3: Hypotheses: technical support should be built in, users should see clearly where their content is, they need a space to share opinions and simple access to what suits their taste.
spotify.lean.l4: Solutions: a payment section inside the app, visible comments on albums, podcasts and episodes, a 1 to 5 rating, saving to a specific place with a reminder, and mini trailers.
spotify.lean.l5: Business outcomes aimed for: raise the app rating from 4.8 to 5.0 in 6 months, increase retention by 10% in 3 months and gain 5% more subscriptions per month over 6 months.
spotify.lean.l6: User benefits: clarity on payment, certainty about where things are saved, time saved and problems solved more simply.
spotify.lean.l7: Most important to learn: whether the app is confusing, whether users get frustrated when they can't find a solution, and whether they really want to give their opinion. Next: interview, prototype, test.
spotify.ia.b2: To test it, I ran a card sorting with one card missing from the current architecture: TECHNICAL SUPPORT. Participants grouped it with Settings, Edit, Security and privacy, Audio and video quality and Frequently asked questions.
spotify.ia.b3: Participants organised the cards around three categories:
spotify.ia.c1: Profile: personalisation, sign out, technical support, security and privacy.
spotify.ia.c2: Search: finding friends, discoveries, music and podcast categories.
spotify.ia.c3: My library: downloaded music and podcasts, favourites.
spotify.ia.s1: Two conclusions came out of it. First, the architecture can be reorganised: Spotify offers many well connected categories for finding content, but product and profile management topics remain disconnected, making the goal hard to reach.
spotify.ia.s2: Second, adding technical support and help to the mobile version is viable: users group it with technical and management topics, as in social networks or banking services. Following that mental structure already in place makes the feature easier to find.
spotify.prio.b: Ideas were placed in a prioritisation matrix with MFVD, by desirability for users and feasibility of implementation. Four priority levels came out of it:
spotify.prio.l1: Priority 1: show where a song is saved and choose the list, offer to save a podcast with a simple like, remove filters one by one, search for a song inside an album, sort artists by genre.
spotify.prio.l2: Priority 2: filter podcasts by recently played or unfinished episodes, save an episode to a favourites list, show fun facts about the artist and album, pre-select favourite songs.
spotify.prio.l3: Priority 3: automatically create lists of songs related by genre, organise albums by musical genre, create a dedicated folder for podcasts.
spotify.prio.l4: Priority 4: link a list to a genre, search for an album or song by a saved artist, lists created with AI help, share lists without leaving the platform.
spotify.flow.b2: All three tasks went through these steps. Task A: save a song to a new playlist. Task B: rate a podcast she has just listened to, with or without a comment. Task C: update her payment method, with PayPal or a card, by editing or deleting.
spotify.ds.b: Before the final screens, I set the product's foundations with atomic design: atoms, molecules and organisms that keep the same design qualities everywhere.
spotify.ds.p1: A palette on a black background, with white and cool greys, then five families in five tones each: raspberry, orange, green, blue and coral.
spotify.ds.p2: A scale in em, from 0.8 to 2.441 em, sets the hierarchy of information and brings clarity to each screen.
spotify.ds.p3: The simple line style is kept, but stroke weight and the structure of some functions were reworked to tell states apart more clearly.
spotify.ds.p4: A tab bar with three states (Home, Search, Library), a mini player, song rows, the episode card with its Rate button, podcast cards, settings lists and the bank card.
spotify.alt.testers: The five test participants: Tatiana, Manuel, Kevin, Anderson and Paula
spotify.tests.g1: Rating a podcast: 5 out of 5 participants see a feature that makes them feel part of a community, by giving their opinion and reading others' to find content.
spotify.tests.g2: Saving a song: 5 out of 5 participants note that steps are reduced, which cuts frustration, and that it is clear where the song is saved.
spotify.tests.m1: To improve, payment: 3 out of 5 participants want a clearer message confirming the update of their payment method, to feel “sure”.
spotify.tests.m2: To improve, rating: 2 out of 5 participants would like to simulate typing in the prototype to check the result.
spotify.motion.b: Four animated interactions guide and reassure the user:
spotify.motion.l1: From home to profile: an immediate opening to get there fast, then on return the profile folds back to create a hierarchy between elements.
spotify.motion.l2: Progress: a movement that tells the user they are moving forward in the process.
spotify.motion.l3: Payment confirmation: a loading animation that confirms the card details.
spotify.motion.l4: Saving a song: a movement that makes it clear the action will be easy and quick.
spotify.voice.b: To decide how the product talks to users, I started from the golden circle, which answers three questions:
spotify.voice.l1: Why: let people connect their feelings to the music they like, to artists and to people who matter to them, at any moment and in any place.
spotify.voice.l2: How: by offering a wide variety of content, lists, albums and podcasts, in a digital product people take anywhere.
spotify.voice.l3: What: a streaming platform to find content that matches one's taste, with lists, downloads, group listening sessions, new artists and the latest releases.
spotify.voice.b2: From there came the voice matrix, which defines the brand's personality around four values: quality, efficiency, closeness and clarity. For each one, it sets verbosity, vocabulary, punctuation and capitalisation, for example 70% capitals at the start of words or for artists and 30% to highlight descriptive content.
spotify.voice.b3: Tone follows from voice. A tone matrix makes it vary along the journey, from the home screen to the confirmation of a save, without losing consistency.
spotify.voice.b4: The style guide gathers the writing rules, with good and bad practices:
spotify.voice.g1: Dates: day, month and year in numbers, with 4 digits for the year, or the month written out.
spotify.voice.g2: Success message: clear and friendly, it confirms the process is complete. Example: “Your data has been saved!”.
spotify.voice.g3: Error message: clear and precise, it says what happened and what can be done. Example: “We couldn't update your payment details, please check them and try again.”.
spotify.voice.g4: Input fields: concrete examples of the expected format, such as ejemplo@gmail.com or a card number in groups of four digits.
